sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 covers the industrial north end of Gloucester City along the Delaware River, from the city line with Camden at the top down to Mercer Street, and from the river shore east to Ellis Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. The whole sheet is taken by two large works. The upper half is the Welsbach Company, manufacturers of incandescent gas burners and electric refrigerators, a dense group of brick shops, boiler house, foundry and storage buildings, with a block of fireproof manufacturing and storage buildings along its east side; at its north end a group of buildings is marked as leased to the Furness Corporation, manufacturers of artificial silk, with the Welsbach Company as owner. The lower half is the Ancona Plant of the Armstrong Cork Co., with two large frame warehouses, a receiving and distributing station, and a long range of brick storage buildings near Ellis Street. Railroad sidings, water pipes, hydrants and private fire service lines run between the buildings, and a note on one pipe refers to the force pumps in the Argo Mills. The river shore with its bulkheads and slips is tinted blue along the left edge. A note across the top margin refers to the Camden volume two for the ground north of the sheet.
notes: Placed from one hand-picked junction (Ellis Street / Mercer Street) with the atlas scale and the rotation of Mercer Street (anchored); low confidence until control is carried from sheets 3 and 4.
Welsbach Company works; Furness Corporation artificial silk (lessees); Armstrong Cork Co., Ancona Plant.
Margin note: See Camden Volume Two.

Delaware River waterfront north of Mercer Street: Welsbach Company, Furness Corpn (artificial silk), Armstrong Cork Co. Ancona Plant. 50 ft. No usable junction west of Ellis; placed by two points carried from sheet 4 (Ellis/Mercer block corner, river slip corner): helmert.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 covers the north end of Gloucester City, in the area between Linden and Warren Streets at the top and Mercer Street at the bottom, from Ellis Street on the west to North Broadway on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 33 degrees, so north points to the upper left. The ground is mixed. At the west edge the Armstrong Cork Co. warehouses, labelled Ware Ho. A and Ware Ho. B, stand in a double frame block with a note to see sheet 2 for the rest of the plant, and an open block beside it is blank. Across the top of the middle, a railroad of several tracks (lettered C. G. & Mt. E. R. R., P. & R. Ry.) curves down through the sheet and passes the Passenger Station and Freight Depot with its wooden platform, near Salem Street; a section house and a cement floor building stand along the tracks. North of Warren Street the sheet shows only a few houses on North Willow Street, and the blocks below Salem Street, numbered 14 to 25, are close rows of frame dwellings with a few brick stores and a cinder block building. The Nanette Mfg. Co. knitting factory (Factory No. 4) stands on the north side of Morris Street at North Burlington Street. A margin note reads See Camden, N.J. Volume Two, and the adjoining sheets 2, 4, 5, 6, 16 and 17 are numbered at the edges. Water pipes of 4 to 8 inches and fire hydrants are drawn along the streets.
notes: Streets are printed with N. but without suffixes; the modern names are North King Street, North Burlington Street, North Broadway, North Willow Street and Mercer Street.
North Willow Street is drawn about 8 to 10 m from its modern line in OpenStreetMap and was left out of the control; Salem Street was also left out because railroad tracks run in it.
A margin note reads See Camden, N.J. Volume Two.

Warren to Mercer, Ellis to North Broadway; Armstrong Cork warehouses at the west edge, railroad and station near Salem. 50 ft, grid about -33. Salem and North Willow left out (tracks in street; Willow displaced).

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 covers the Delaware River waterfront of Gloucester City between Mercer Street at the top and Monmouth Street at the bottom, and from the river shore east to North Willow Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 33 degrees, so north points to the upper left. The whole west half is the plant of the Armstrong Cork Co., lettered along its length with its receiving and distributing station, power plant and storage buildings: long brick and pink-coloured warehouses (Ware Ho.), a receiving room, an engine room, a hose house and a knitting-station building stand between Ellis Street and the shore, with sprinklers, fire pumps and an 8 inch water pipe drawn through the plant. A note in the margin says the data for the plant were taken from plans and the office and were not verified. North of the plant a few frame warehouses stand on a lot cut by two slips or docks, with the shore drawn in blue. East of Ellis Street the sheet shows four blocks of attached brick and frame dwellings and stores between Mercer, Middlesex, Hudson and Bergen Streets, one with a bakery, a printing office and a vacant dilapidated building; a candy manufacturer, a lodge hall and an office stand on North King Street, and the block between Ellis and North King Streets south of Bergen Street is a playground with a play house. The adjoining sheets 2, 3, 5 and 7 are numbered at the edges.
notes: Street names are printed with N. and S. but without suffixes; the modern names are North King Street, South King Street, North Willow Street and South Willow Street.
North Willow Street is drawn displaced from its modern line on neighbouring sheets and was left out of the control here.
A margin note says the Armstrong Cork plant data were from plans and office and not verified.
Delaware waterfront, Mercer to Monmouth; Armstrong Cork plant west of Ellis; four blocks and a playground east. 50 ft. North Willow left out.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 covers the central business blocks of Gloucester City, between Mercer Street at the top and Monmouth Street at the bottom and from North and South Willow Streets on the west to North and South Sussex Streets on the east, with Burlington Street running down the middle. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 33 degrees, so north points to the upper left. Middlesex, Hudson and Bergen Streets cross it, giving a regular grid of blocks numbered 29 to 46. Most of the blocks are rows of frame and brick dwellings with stores, among them rows of attached brick houses and shops east of Burlington Street. The civic and commercial buildings are concentrated around Burlington and Bergen Streets: City Hall and the Fire Department with its hose tower on Monmouth Street, the City Hotel, the Leader motion picture theatre, a dance hall, a pool room and a garage for twenty cars, the First Presbyterian Church, and the American Legion club house on Hudson Street. A short block of North Broadway and Plum Street appears at the upper right edge, and the margin carries the numbers of the adjoining sheets 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 16. Water pipes of 4 to 16 inches and fire hydrants are drawn in the streets.
notes: Burlington, Willow and Sussex are printed with N. and S. but without suffixes; the modern names are North and South Burlington Street, North and South Willow Street and North and South Sussex Street.
North Willow Street is drawn displaced from its modern line (junctions 3 to 5 m off) and was left out of the control.
Central blocks, Mercer to Monmouth, Willow to Sussex; City Hall, fire department. 50 ft. North Willow left out (modern line skewed 3 to 5 m).

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the part of Gloucester City on both sides of North Broadway between Mercer Street at the top and Monmouth Street at the bottom, from West Sussex Street at the west edge to Champion Road and the Railroad Avenue tracks at the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. The sheet joins two street grids: west of Broadway the blocks (31, 32, 37, 42, 47) follow the downtown grid of sheets 3 to 5 and run square to the page, while east of Broadway the streets (Mercer, Middlesex, Chambers Avenue, Hudson, Paul, Bergen) and the blocks 173 to 182 are turned about 33 degrees from them and run square to the railroad. The railroad tracks of the W. J. & S. R. R. and the P. R. R. run from the top of the sheet to the lower right alongside Railroad Avenue. Buildings of note include the Broadway School and its annex on Mercer Street, C. H. Craig and Sons tallow rendering works on Middlesex Street at North Broadway, the Gloucester City Trust Co. bank at the upper left, the Knights of Columbus club house on Monmouth Street, a garage for twenty-five cars on Bergen Street, the Monmouth Street Public School, the First M. E. Church and Bible School, the post office and the Republican Club. Dwellings are mostly frame, with rows of attached brick houses along Paul Street and Champion Road. Water pipes of 4 to 16 inches are drawn in the streets. The margin carries the numbers of sheets 5, 7, 8, 9, 16, 17 and 3.
notes: Sussex is printed as W. Sussex; the modern street is North Sussex Street.
Fillmore is spelled Filmore in OpenStreetMap (North Filmore Street).
Railroad Avenue was left out of the control because the railroad tracks run in it; Bergen Street at North Sussex Street and at North Broadway was excluded as a poor detection.
Both sides of North Broadway, Mercer to Monmouth; two street grids about 33 degrees apart, one part. 50 ft. Railroad Avenue (tracks in street) left out.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 covers the south end of the downtown waterfront and the blocks east of it, between Monmouth Street at the top and Market Street at the bottom, from the Delaware River shore to Burlington Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 36 degrees. The west half is industrial: on Monmouth Street stand the Empire Tool Corp'n toy and tool works and, behind it, the American Diaton Co. refining diatomaceous earth and The John M. Rogers Works (lessee) making small tools, with a machine shop, a boiler house and a wooden water tank. Below them the U.S. Commission of Immigration's Gloucester Immigrant Station occupies a detention house and buildings in a loop of open galleries (block 48), reached by a lane from Monmouth Street. The south-west corner is the Stinson and Dickensheets coal and lumber yard, with lumber piles, sheds, a planing mill and an old dock on the river front. Land north of the yard is marked as solid fill. East of South King Street the sheet shows residential and commercial blocks 49, 50, 54, 55, 59, 59 1/2 and 64: St. Mary's R.C. High School, the first M. E. Church, the Apollo Moving Picture Theatre, the Keystone Telephone Exchange, a bank, the Hotel Dixie, and rows of frame dwellings on Somerset, Cumberland and Ridge Avenue. The margin carries the numbers of sheets 4, 5, 8, 11, 13 and 9.
notes: Street names are printed with N. and S. but without suffixes; the modern names are South King Street, North Willow Street, South Willow Street, North Burlington Street and South Burlington Street.
Ridge Av. is the modern Ridgeway Street; it is drawn at a slant not matched by the modern line and was left out of the control.
North Willow Street and South Willow Street at Monmouth and Somerset Streets are about 8 to 9 m from their modern line and were left out of the control.
Waterfront industry (Empire Tool, Immigrant Station, Stinson and Dickensheets lumber) and blocks to Burlington; turned about -36. 50 ft. Control on South King and South Burlington only.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 covers four blocks of central Gloucester City between Monmouth Street on the north and Market Street on the south, and between Burlington Street on the west and Atlantic Street on the east, with Sussex Street dividing the area in two. Somerset, Cumberland and Ridgeway Streets cross it parallel to Monmouth. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 37 degrees on the page, so north points to the upper left. The district is residential: long rows of frame dwellings, many with rear sheds and stables, line every block, with brick rows at the Burlington Street and Sussex Street corners and a few stores among them. The sheet is the parish centre of the town. St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church and its priest's house stand on Monmouth Street at the corner of Atlantic Street; St. Mary's School and the convent face Cumberland and Ridgeway Streets east of the middle of block 60; the First Baptist Church stands at Monmouth and Sussex Streets, and the Church of the Ascension (Episcopal) on Cumberland Street east of Sussex Street. A row of small buildings on Monmouth Street holds the Crescent Appliance Co., manufacturing. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches are drawn along the streets, with fire hydrants and the fire alarm box at Burlington and Market Streets. Ridge Avenue is shown entering from the west at the left edge. Block numbers 51, 52, 56, 57, 60, 61, 65 and 66 are printed, and the margins name the adjoining sheets 5, 6, 7, 9, 12 and 13.
notes: Burlington and Sussex are printed with N. and S. but without a suffix; the modern streets are South Burlington Street and South Sussex Street.
Monmouth, Somerset, Cumberland, Ridgeway, Market and Atlantic are printed without a suffix; today they are streets of the same names.
Pilot. Monmouth to Market, Burlington to Atlantic Streets; St. Mary's R.C. Church, First Baptist Church. 50 ft, grid turned about 37 degrees.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 covers the south-eastern part of the downtown, between Monmouth Street at the top and Market Street at the bottom, from Atlantic Street on the west to Filmore Street and the Railroad Avenue tracks on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Like sheet 6 it joins two street grids: west of South Broadway the blocks (53, 58, 62, 67, 68) run square to the page and are the downtown grid turned about 37 degrees from north, while east of Broadway the streets (Champion Road, Ridgeway, Filmore) and blocks 138, 145 to 148 are turned about 33 degrees from it and run square to the railroad. Cumberland Street is drawn with a long oval park or loop in its middle west of Joy Street. The notable buildings are the Ridgeway Public School and the Gloucester City High School (fireproof, built 1925) on Cumberland and Ridgeway Streets, the Gloucester City Trust Co. bank at Monmouth Street, the Knights of Columbus club house, the passenger station and freight house of the W. J. & S. R. R. beside Railroad Avenue, a coal shed and a large vacant lot, and the Broadway Garage and an auto sales and service building on South Broadway. Most blocks are rows of frame dwellings with a few stores. Sixth and Seventh Streets are shown as paper streets at the foot of the sheet. The margin carries the numbers of sheets 6, 8, 10, 13, 17 and 19.
notes: Broadway is printed N. Broadway and S. Broadway; the modern streets are North Broadway and South Broadway.
Filmore is spelled as OpenStreetMap does (South Filmore Street); the junction with Cumberland Street was left out of the control.
Cumberland Street west of South Broadway is drawn with an oval in its middle and was left out of the control; Atlantic Street at the west edge was also left out because only half of it is drawn.
Monmouth to Market, Atlantic to Filmore; Ridgeway Public School, high school, passenger station; two grids. 50 ft.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 covers the district of Gloucester City south of Monmouth Street and west of Westminster Avenue, between a band of railroad tracks on the west and Westminster Avenue on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 37 degrees on the page, so north points to the upper left. The top of the sheet shows the south side of Monmouth Street with a row of dwellings between Railroad Avenue and Brown Street, and the Brown St. Public School stands at the corner of Brown and the block marked 151. Somerset Street, Little Somerset (E. Brown) and Cumberland Street cross the sheet from west to east, with rows of frame dwellings, a few stores and sheds, and block numbers 149, 150, 151 and 152. Washington Avenue runs diagonally south from Somerset to Market Street past the J. R. Quigley Co. lumber, building material yard, whose long mill and lumber sheds and warehouses fill the centre of the lower sheet. West of the yard the Railroad Avenue tracks run in a broad band down the left side, and beside them stand the Stinson Dickensheets Inc. lumber yard with its long lumber shed, a cement and lime warehouse, and a cluster of small shops and sheds along Fillmore Street and South Broadway at the lower left. An office and storage building stands on Market Street at the bottom edge. Westminster Avenue is the heavy line along the right margin, where the pipe and house numbers of the next block begin. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches and several fire hydrants are drawn in the streets. The adjoining sheets are numbered 9, 17, 18 and 19 in the margins.
notes: Printed Somerset west of Washington Avenue is today Little Somerset Street, and the printed Little Somerset (E. Brown) is today East Brown Street.
The Monmouth, Somerset, Cumberland and Market streets are printed without a suffix; the modern streets bear the same names with Street.
Printed South Brown is South Brown Street; Westminster Avenue is Westminster Street in OpenStreetMap, but its modern line is displaced from the drawn one and was not used for control.
Printed Fillmore is South Filmore Street today (spelling differs).
Brown Street at its junction with E. Brown (modern East Brown / Westminster) is drawn several metres from the modern junction and was left out of the control.
Monmouth to Market, Railroad Av to Westminster Av; J. R. Quigley lumber yard. 50 ft. Westminster and South Filmore left out (displaced).

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 shows the Delaware River frontage of Gloucester City from Market Street south to the ferry landing and Water Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 38 degrees, so north points to the upper left. Only the strip along the right-hand side is built up: four blocks, numbered 70, 77, 83 and part of 69, between South King Street and South Burlington Street and between Market and Jersey Avenue. They hold rows of frame and brick dwellings, the Elk Home, a garage, a wagon shed, Coyle's Hotel at King Street and Jersey Avenue, and a number of stores. The Public Service Corporation of New Jersey Gloucester Sub-Station stands at the upper left of block 69 beside the Camden County Memorial Park, which occupies the shore land with its Swimming Pool and Club House. West of the park the river bank is drawn with piers and slips; the Gloucester Ferry Co. South St. Line (not in operation) buildings, with a planing and carpenter shop and waiting room, stand on the old ferry pier. Ferry Avenue runs from the shore to Jersey Avenue and the unbuilt blocks 99 and 100. Below, Water Street and 3rd Street cross near the Mansion House and the Community House, which stand on block 100 and block 101. The Delaware River is lettered down the left edge. Water mains are drawn in the streets, with hydrants and a fire alarm box at Jersey Avenue. The adjoining sheets are numbered 7, 12 and 14.
notes: Printed South Burlington is the street now called 3rd Street (OpenStreetMap) north of Jersey Avenue.
The printed 3rd Street runs through the Water Street junction near the bottom right; Water is printed without a suffix.
Ferry Avenue is not in the OpenStreetMap extract and was not used for control.
The Mansion House and Community House are named on the sheet; the Gloucester Ferry Co. buildings are marked not in operation.
Control points on South Burlington Street (3rd Street) were hand-picked because the sheet edge cuts the street and the detector paired a lot line.
Delaware front, Market to Jersey Av, S. King to S. Burlington (today 3rd Street); Camden County Memorial Park. 50 ft. Four hand-picked points on 3rd Street and Water.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers the centre of Gloucester City, from Market Street south to Jersey Avenue and Water Street, and from South Burlington Street east to 5th Street. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 38 degrees, so north points to the upper left. Four rows of blocks, numbered 71, 72, 78, 79, 84, 85, 102 and 105, lie between Market, Powell, Hunter Streets and Jersey Avenue. They are filled with frame dwellings and brick rows, with stores on the street fronts. Distinctive buildings include the Lodge Rooms and a hall on Market Street, the German Luth'n Church on 4th Street, John F. Zinner's beer bottling works on Jersey Avenue, and the Atlantic Ice Mfg. Co. ice plant with its engine and dynamo room on the east side of block 85. A large garage with a show room stands on Jersey Avenue at Walnut Street, and the New Year's Club and several second hand furniture storage buildings face Jersey Avenue at 5th Street. Jersey Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally from the upper left to the lower right and is the line at which the grid is bent; south of it are the old lots of Water Street, 4th Street, Walnut Street and Spruce Street. Division Street and the 5th Street edge are at the right. Water mains of 4, 6 and 8 inches, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are drawn in the streets. The adjoining sheets are numbered 8, 11, 13 and 14.
notes: Printed South Burlington is the street now called 3rd Street (OpenStreetMap).
Water, Walnut and Spruce are printed without a suffix; today Walnut is Pine Street and Spruce is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
The printed S. Sussex at the top margin is today South Sussex Street.
Market to Jersey Av, S. Burlington (3rd Street) to 5th St; Atlantic Ice Mfg Co. 50 ft.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 lies south-east of the centre of Gloucester City, between Market Street at the top and Jersey Avenue at the bottom, and between 5th Street on the west and 7th Street on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 37 degrees, so north points to the upper left. The upper two rows of blocks, numbered 73, 74, 80 and 81, are lined with frame and brick dwellings, stores and a milk depot (Supplee-Wills-Jones) on Market Street. The largest feature is the Breslin Bros. Carpet Co. Inc. mill, whose Mills Nos. 1, 2 and 3, dye houses, engine house, boiler room, machine shop and pump house fill block 80 between Powell and Hunter Streets. South of Hunter Street the blocks, numbered 86 and 87, hold Foster's Laundry, a garment factory, the Hunter St. School and scattered dwellings, but much of the land is open. Below Division Street the blocks marked 94, 94 1/2 and 94 2 are laid out but empty, bounded by Jersey Avenue and Cherry Street, which cross the lower part of the sheet in broad diagonals. The left edge shows a small part of block 14 and the street lettered Ann. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches are shown in the streets with hydrants. The adjoining sheets are numbered 8, 9, 12, 14 and 19.
notes: The mill is lettered Breslin Bros. Carpet Co. Inc.; the Hunter St. School is on 6th Street.
Cherry Street at 7th Street is drawn several metres from the modern line and was left out of the control.
Market to Jersey Av, 5th to 7th St; Breslin Bros carpet works. 50 ft.

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 covers the south-west part of Gloucester City between 4th Street at the top and Charles Street at the bottom, and from Water Street in the west to 6th Street and Jersey Avenue in the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid nearly square to the page, north up and slightly to the left. Most of the upper half is laid out with blocks numbered 103, 104, 106, 107, 108 and 109, whose lots are ruled but which carry few buildings: a building marked vacant on 4th Street, a small group of dwellings on the block at 5th Street, an auto repair shop, and open land with storage of old autos and old lumber. Walnut Street and Spruce Street run north and south, Water Street along the west side. The south-east is filled by the industry of The Hinde & Dauch Paper Co., Mfrs. of Paper Boxes: pink brick paper mill, machine room, beater room, stock room, warehouses and a long paper storage building, with a frame trestle at the east edge. At the south-west The Lang Co. engine and dynamo room, its steel water tower and an elevated 50,000 gallon tank stand beside a note referring to sheet 15; a store house stands on the north side of Charles Street, which runs diagonally across the lower left. The next sheets are numbered 12, 13, 15 and 19. Water mains of 6 and 10 inches and hydrants are drawn in the streets.
notes: The printed Walnut is today Pine Street, and the printed 6th Street is 6th Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Charles Street at Pine Street is drawn off the modern line and was left out of the control.
The Lang Co. buildings continue on sheet 15 (printed note: For report see sheet No. 15).
4th St to Charles St, Water to 6th St; Hinde and Dauch Paper Co., The Lang Co. engine room. 50 ft, north up.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 covers the industrial waterfront at the south end of Gloucester City along the Delaware River, drawn at 100 feet to an inch; its streets are turned about 11 degrees anticlockwise against those of sheet 14, which it adjoins at the top right. Water Street runs down the right-hand side from Charles Street, which enters at the upper right beside Walnut Street and a cluster of railroad tracks; 6th Street touches the top edge. Almost the whole sheet is taken by three works. At the top, between the river and Water Street, stands The Lang Co., manufacturers of felt base roofing paper, with its paper machine and beater room, warehouse, fuel oil tanks and a slip from the river. Below it lie the buildings of the American Radiator Co., including a long foundry and machine shop marked not in operation, and the Port of Philadelphia Terminals, a fenced yard reaching out to the river with a pier and a line of ship gantries numbered 1 to 4 at the lower left, served by a web of railroad sidings. East of Water Street the lower right is the yard of the Pusey and Jones Co., largely open ground with one frame building. Hydrants, water pipes and a mill service water tank are drawn along Water Street. The river shore and the slips are tinted blue. There is almost no housing on the sheet.
notes: Placed from one point carried from sheet 14 (north-east corner of Water and Charles Streets) with the atlas scale for 100 ft sheets (3.939 px/ft) and a rotation of -11 degrees measured from Water Street and Charles Street against sheet 14 (anchored); low confidence, errors grow towards the bottom of the sheet.
The north arrow on this sheet (about -5 degrees) does not agree with the streets; it was not used.
The Lang Co. felt base roofing paper works; American Radiator Co. foundry not in operation; Port of Philadelphia Terminals; Pusey and Jones Co. yard.

Waterfront south of Charles Street: The Lang Co., American Radiator Co., Port of Philadelphia Terminals, Pusey & Jones Co. 100 ft. No usable junction; anchored on one point carried from sheet 14 (north-east corner of Water and Charles) at 3.939 px/ft and north_deg -11 (measured from Water and Charles Streets against sheet 14; the sheet's north arrow, about -5, disagrees). Low confidence, errors grow towards the bottom of the sheet.

sheet-16-1.description: The main part of sheet 16 covers the north end of Gloucester City at 100 feet to an inch, from North King Street and Linden Street at the upper left to Johnson Street on the east, and from Passaic Street south to Mercer Street. North Broadway runs down the west side and the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway), Grenloch Branch, runs north and south through the middle with Railroad Avenue on both sides of the tracks; a branch curves east along the south side of the South Branch of Newton Creek, which crosses the upper right. The built-up part is the strip along North Broadway, with close rows of brick and frame dwellings and stores on Sherman, Warren, Salem, Essex and Morris Streets, and short rows of dwellings east of the railroad on Essex, Morris and Mercer Streets as far as Brown and Johnson Streets. Industry is represented by the Forrest Mercerizing Co. mill at Salem Street and Fillmore Street beside the railroad, a lumber yard and woodworking shop on Salem Street, and P. Mealy's Sons hides and tallow works on North King Street, with auto painting and auto repair shops near it. Much of the land east of the railroad and north of Essex Street is shown as open blocks. Water pipes and hydrants are drawn along the streets. A note at the upper left refers to the Camden volume two for the area beyond the city line. The upper right of the page holds a separate part (part 2) bounded by a heavy line.
notes: Johnson is today North Johnson Boulevard; Brown is North Brown Street; Railroad Avenue is East and West Railroad Avenue on either side of the tracks.
Fillmore is not in the modern street data at this point.
Margin note: See Camden Volume Two.

Two parts at 100 ft: part 1 North Broadway to Johnson Street, Passaic to Mercer (north end); part 2 inset in the upper right (heavy line): Market Street from Birch to Spruce Avenues near the Mount Ephraim line, mostly unopened streets.

sheet-16-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 16 is an inset in the upper right of the page, set off by a heavy line, showing a sparsely built tract on Market Street at the east end of Gloucester City near the Mount Ephraim line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north to the upper left. Market Street crosses the top of the inset; Birch, Walnut, Maple, Chestnut, Cypress and Spruce Avenues run south from it, and Orange, Cedar, Park and Weston Avenues run north of it. Oriental Avenue closes the inset along its lower edge. Several of these streets are marked as not opened (Birch, Oriental, Orange, Cedar and Weston Avenues), so the inset is largely a plan of laid-out lots with only scattered frame dwellings, mostly along Walnut Avenue and on Market Street. The Homestead Inn stands on the south side of Market Street between Walnut and Maple Avenues. A few dwellings and a garage stand north of Market Street near Park Avenue and along Spruce Avenue. Lot numbers are printed along Walnut Avenue, and block numbers 396 to 412 mark the blocks. No buildings of industry or institutions are drawn.
notes: Placed from four junctions along Market Street only (helmert); Oriental Avenue today does not follow its drawn line (hand-picked Birch and Maple junctions on it disagreed by 11 to 36 m) and was left out, as was Chestnut Avenue, whose modern line is not where it is drawn.
Homestead Inn on Market Street.

Two parts at 100 ft: part 1 North Broadway to Johnson Street, Passaic to Mercer (north end); part 2 inset in the upper right (heavy line): Market Street from Birch to Spruce Avenues near the Mount Ephraim line, mostly unopened streets.

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 covers the north-central part of Gloucester City between Mercer Street at the top and Somerset Street at the bottom, and between the Railroad Avenue tracks on the west and the Gloucester Station railroad and Newton Creek on the east. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north roughly up the page. The upper half is a regular grid: Mercer, Middlesex, Chambers and Paul Streets cross it from west to east, with N. Brown Street and Johnson Street running north and south and Gaunt Street ending at Johnson. Blocks 183, 184, 178, 179, 174, 175, 170 and 171 are filled with frame dwellings, many of them two storeys with rear sheds, and a row of attached brick or frame houses stands on the south side of Paul Street at the left. South of Paul the streets turn to run diagonally from upper left to lower right: Hudson, Bergen, Monmouth and Somerset Streets cross S. Brown and Johnson Streets, and the blocks numbered 164, 163, 166, 169, 154 and 155 are lined with frame and some brick dwellings. At the left edge the Railroad Avenue tracks (W. J. & S. R. R.) run down the page beside Railroad Av., with Champion Rd. cutting across them. At the right, the Atlantic City Railroad (P. & R. Ry., Grenloch Branch) runs beside Johnson Street. East of it are the Gloucester City Water Works with a reservoir of 1 1/2 million gallons and a settling basin, the Gloucester Gun Club, the J. R. Quigley Co. lumber yard, and C. C. Coolbraugh and Son's wholesale millwork and planing mill on Nicholson Rd. Newton Creek, with its South Branch, curves across the right side. Highland Blvd. enters at the lower right. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 20 inches are marked, and the adjoining sheets 16, 6, 9, 10 and 18 are named at the margins.
notes: Railroad Avenue is printed Railroad Av. beside the tracks; the modern streets are East Railroad Avenue and West Railroad Avenue.

North Brown and South Brown (printed N. Brown, S. Brown) are North Brown Street and South Brown Street today; Johnson is North Johnson Boulevard and South Johnson Boulevard; Chambers is Chambers Avenue.
The printed scale bar reads 100 ft to one inch; the fitted scale is about 3.97 px per foot.
Mercer to Somerset, Brown, Johnson, Railroad Av; Newton Creek; water works. 100 ft, north up.

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 covers the district of Gloucester City around Market Street and the Cedar Grove Cemetery, from Somerset Street and Highland Boulevard at the top to Thompson Avenue at the bottom, and from Westminster Avenue at the left to Baynes Avenue, Hickman Avenue and Amon Avenue at the right. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch; the street grid is turned about 30 degrees on the page and the north arrow points to the upper left. At the top left, Somerset Street, East Brown Street, Katherine and Frances Streets form a group of blocks (156 and 157) of frame dwellings, some of them in brick rows, with the Atlantic City Railroad (P. & R. Ry., Grenloch Branch) curving across the top. A pond and a lake lie north of Baynes Avenue. In the middle, Mary Street and Ridgeway Street border St. Mary's Cemetery, which fills the open ground to the west, and Market Street runs across the sheet with stores, a fire alarm box and the H. W. Walker and Son concrete block manufactory on its south side. Below Market, Barnard Avenue, Lane Avenue, Stinson Avenue, Harley Avenue and Burdsall Avenue are lined with small frame houses in blocks 214, 215, 283, 414, 216 and 217, with Powell, Hunter and Thompson Streets crossing them. Cedar Grove Cemetery occupies the large open wedge at the lower right. At the right, Sparks Avenue, Barnaby Avenue, Hickman Avenue and Amon Avenue curve through the new blocks 251, 252, 253 and 254, which are still thinly built. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 16 inches are drawn along the streets, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The adjoining sheets named at the margins are 17, 10, 19, 20 and 23. The Princeton University Library map division stamp appears at the lower right.
notes: Katherine and Frances are Kathryn Street and Francis Street today; Mary is St Mary's Street; Hunter is Little Hunter Street; Stinson, Harley and Burdsall are North Stinson, North Harley and North Burdsall Avenues; Lane Avenue, Market Street and Thompson Avenue keep their names.
Market Street is drawn 50 feet wide and its modern line is a few metres off the drawn centre; two Market Street junctions (Lane and Sparks) were hand-picked on the drawn edges.
Market and Cedar Grove Cemetery district (Lane, Barnard, Stinson, Harley, Burdsall, Baynes, Sparks). 100 ft, about -30. Two hand-picked points on Market.

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 covers the south-western part of Gloucester City from Market Street at the top to Charles Street and the undeveloped blocks to its south, and from the 6th Street railroad siding at the left to Stites Avenue and Barnard Avenue at the right. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 37 degrees on the page, so north points to the upper left. The upper left is a regular grid of residential blocks (75, 82, 88, 89, 91 and 92) between Powell, Hunter and Division Streets and 7th and 8th Streets, with frame dwellings and a few stores, and a church on 8th Street in block 88. South Broadway runs diagonally from the top to the lower right beside the railroad and Union Cemetery, which fills the wedge between the tracks and South Broadway; small frame houses line its west side, with John Street, George Street and the J. J. Wolf bottling works near the lower right. Gallagher Bros. Inc. occupies the ground beside the railroad at the top. In the middle, Center Avenue, Cherry Street and Jersey Avenue cross the sheet and the Jersey Av. Public School stands between 8th Street and Cherry Street. At the lower left C. A. Marshall's lumber shed and wood-working plant lies on Charles Street, and the blocks south of Charles Street (116 to 122) carry the streets Pine, Cedar, Grove, Elm and Brick, most of them marked as not open and unbuilt. Kohler Street leaves South Broadway at the lower right near a garage. At the right edge Stites Avenue and Barnard Avenue run down a strip of detached houses. The margin carries the legend No Exposure at the bottom, and the adjoining sheets 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 18 and 20 are named.
notes: Several streets south of Charles Street (Pine, Cedar, Grove, Elm, 9th Street, 10th Street) are marked Not Open on the sheet.

The modern 8th Street, 9th Street, Cherry Street and Center Street junctions sit 6 to 10 m off the drawn ones in this part, so they were left out of the fit; Division Street at South Broadway was also left out as an acute junction.
Kohler is spelled Koehler Street in OpenStreetMap; Center Av. is Center Street today.

Powell to Charles, 7th to Stites; South Broadway, Union Cemetery. 100 ft (scan 8964 px wide, px_per_ft 4.1). 8th, 9th, Cherry, Center left out (modern lines 6 to 10 m off). Scanned larger (10654 px high against 10100), so px_per_ft 4.12 equals 3.90 at the usual scan size; not drawn off scale.

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 covers the southern edge of Gloucester City where it meets the Little Timber Creek. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with the north arrow pointing nearly straight up the page. At the upper left, South Broadway runs down the page past Koehler Street and St. John Street, where small shops and works stand: a row of stores on Koehler Street, a bakery, the Lantern Inn, an auto drive and transmission company, an auto repair shop, a battery station and the Air Reduction Sales Co., maker of acetylene gas. The Atlantic City Railroad (W. J. & S. R. R. and P. R. R.) runs the full height of the sheet beside Railroad Av., with S. Gloucester Station near the top, and a freight line of the P. R. R. curves away to the right across open ground. At the upper centre a set of blocks (218, 219, 230) is laid out on diagonal streets: Lane Av., Stinson Av., Harley Av. and Burdsall Av. cross Thompson Av., with small frame houses on the western ones and Uibell Av. and the lots beyond them (221, 222) still empty. Little Timber Creek crosses the sheet from left to right, spanned by an iron bridge on South Broadway, and its course marks the city limits. South of the creek, B. Goodman and Sons' feed mill and storage stand beside New Broadway and Broadway, and the Browning Plan occupies the lower right: Lake Drive curves round it, with 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th Streets and Center Street laid out in blocks 273 to 277, nearly all unbuilt and marked not open. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 16 inches are drawn along the streets. The adjoining sheets named at the margins are 19, 18, 21 and 22.
notes: St. John is St John Street today; Lane Av., Stinson Av., Harley Av. and Burdsall Av. are Lane Avenue, North and South Stinson, Harley and Burdsall Avenues; Koehler is Koehler Street.
The north-eastern streets (Harley, Burdsall) are drawn slightly closer together than their modern positions; the Thompson Avenue junctions fit within about 3 m.
Part of the Browning Plan streets are marked Not Open on the sheet.

Koehler and South Broadway, Thompson Av, Little Timber Creek, Browning Plan (Lake Drive). 100 ft, north up (larger scan, px_per_ft 4.2). Scanned larger (10654 px high), px_per_ft 4.21 equals 3.99 at the usual scan size.

sheet-23-1.description: The main part of sheet 23 shows Highland Park, the residential development east of the older city on the south side of the South Branch of Newton Creek, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 35 degrees so that north points to the upper left. Klemm Avenue and the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) run along the creek at the top; Highland Boulevard, Park Avenue and Sherwood Avenue cross the sheet parallel to them; Greenwood, Rosalind, Sylvan, Orlando and Palace Avenues run down from Klemm Avenue to Sherwood Avenue and Market Street at the bottom. Amon and Baynes Avenues lie in the lower left beside a creek, and Crescent Boulevard crosses the upper right, east of the marsh that fills the middle of the right half. The area is mostly laid out in lots with detached frame dwellings, densest along Highland Boulevard, Rosalind and Greenwood Avenues and around Baynes Avenue, and many lots are still vacant, especially east of Orlando Avenue. Buildings of note are the Highland Park Fire Department and a Presbyterian church on Highland Boulevard, a sewage disposal plant beside the creek at Klemm Avenue, and a sign manufacturing and painting shop near the lower edge. In the upper right, beyond Crescent Boulevard, a row of dwellings faces Highland Boulevard west of Myrtle Avenue. The lower right of the page holds a separate part (part 2) bounded by a heavy line.
notes: Rosalind Avenue is printed with the older name Roseland Avenue in brackets.
Palace Avenue is not in the modern street data (gone under the Crescent Boulevard and North-South Freeway interchange).
Park Avenue / Rosalind Avenue was rejected (5 m or more off the fit).

Two parts at 100 ft: part 1 Highland Park (Klemm Av to Market, Greenwood to Crescent Blvd); part 2 in the lower right inside a heavy line, drawn at another angle: Highland Blvd east of Myrtle Av, Highland Park Public School, Cloverdale Country Club. Part 2 placed by three points along Highland Boulevard (one carried from part 1, two hand-picked on paper streets): helmert, 3.7 m RMSE, low confidence; second pass keep.

sheet-23-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 23 occupies the lower right of the page, inside a heavy line, and continues Highland Boulevard east of Myrtle Avenue toward Park Avenue at 100 feet to an inch, drawn at a different angle from the main part with its own north arrow. Highland Boulevard crosses the part from the upper left to the lower right, lined on its north side by a row of frame dwellings numbered 901 to 933 and on the south by a few more; Fern Avenue (not open) and Ivy Avenue run south from it, and it bends into Park Avenue at the lower right. The Highland Park Public School stands at the corner of Highland Boulevard and Park Avenue. The upper half of the part is taken by the Cloverdale Country Club, with its clubhouse near the top, a private road along the east side, and the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) Grenloch Branch crossing from the left with Cloverdale Station beside Park Avenue. The scale bar of the sheet is printed at the lower left of the part.
notes: Placed by a helmert fit on three hand-picked junctions along Highland Boulevard (Myrtle, Fern and Park Avenues); the three disagree by about 4 m with any similarity fit, so the modern boulevard may not follow its 1930 line here. Low confidence.
Ivy Avenue is not in the modern street data.
Cloverdale Country Club and Cloverdale Station on the Grenloch Branch.

Two parts at 100 ft: part 1 Highland Park (Klemm Av to Market, Greenwood to Crescent Blvd); part 2 in the lower right inside a heavy line, drawn at another angle: Highland Blvd east of Myrtle Av, Highland Park Public School, Cloverdale Country Club. Part 2 placed by three points along Highland Boulevard (one carried from part 1, two hand-picked on paper streets): helmert, 3.7 m RMSE, low confidence; second pass keep.

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 covers the western part of Gloucester Heights, a thinly built district on the eastern edge of Gloucester City between Newton Creek and its South Branch. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north nearly straight up the page. Nicholson Rd. crosses the sheet from the Concrete Bridge over the South Branch at the left to the right edge, and Lehigh Av. and Jefferson Av. cross it to the north; Temple Av., University Av., Rutgers Av., Harvard Av., Oxford Av. and, in the south, Haverford Av. run across them. Most of the ground is open lots (blocks 361 to 363, 377 to 379) with detached frame dwellings strung along Nicholson Rd., Rutgers Av. and Harvard Av. and along Oxford Av., where a row of houses faces the street. Gloucester Heights Fire Ass'n No. 4 has its fire department building on Oxford Av., and the M. E. Church stands on the south side of Nicholson Rd. near the right edge. West of Temple Av. a large cinder block building houses an auto truck repairing and steel truss works. At the top right a dancing pavilion stands north of Lehigh Av. Large areas on the left and in the centre are marked marsh, bordered by dashed tidal lines, and the creeks wind across the sheet. A note at the upper left states that the house numbers on this sheet are arbitrary. The adjoining sheets named at the margins are 17, 23 and 25.
notes: Printed street names carry no suffix besides Av. and Rd.; the modern streets are Nicholson Road, Temple Avenue, University Avenue, Rutgers Avenue, Jefferson Avenue, Lehigh Avenue, Harvard Avenue, Oxford Avenue and Haverford Avenue.
Harvard Avenue and Haverford Avenue no longer reach Nicholson Road; the North-South Freeway (Route 42) now cuts diagonally across the lower right of the sheet.
House numbers on this sheet are arbitrary, as the sheet states.
Gloucester Heights west: Nicholson Rd, Lehigh, Jefferson, Rutgers, Temple, University, Harvard. 100 ft.

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 covers the eastern part of Gloucester Heights, the thinly built district at the eastern edge of Gloucester City, from the tidal Newton Creek at the top to Washington Av. at the bottom, and from Haverford Av. at the left to the Haddon Township line near Greenridge Av. at the right. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north nearly straight up the page. Nicholson Rd. crosses the sheet from left to right, with Lehigh Av. and Barlow Av. parallel to it to the north and Oxford Av., Princeton Av., Yale Av., Cornell Av., Swarthmore Av. and Haverford Av. crossing it. Marlborough Av. runs across the right side. The lots are large and mostly empty, in blocks 356, 357, 364 to 367 and 380 to 382, with scattered frame dwellings along the avenues; three frame houses with brick pink fronts stand on Yale Av. north of Marlborough Av. Public School No. 4, Gloucester Heights, a two-storey fire proof building of brick with concrete floors built in 1923 and 1925, stands on the south side of Nicholson Rd. A filling station stands near Marlborough Av. at the right. The south-eastern part, beyond Crescent Blvd., is a plan of narrow blocks (383 to 388) between Wilson Av., Lincoln Av. and Washington Av., nearly all unbuilt. Hillside Av. and Industrial Av. enter at the upper right near Newton Creek. A note states that house numbers on this sheet are arbitrary. The adjoining sheets named at the margins are 24 and 23.
notes: Swarthmore Av. is Swathmore Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Marlborough is Marlborough Avenue; Greenridge is Green Ridge Avenue today.

The modern Crescent Boulevard and the streets east of Yale Avenue do not follow the drawn plan; including them raised the fit error from 0.6 m to 2.4 m, so the junctions east of Yale Avenue and the Lehigh and Yale junction were left out.
House numbers on this sheet are arbitrary, as the sheet states.
Gloucester Heights east: Oxford, Princeton, Yale, Lehigh, Barlow, Marlborough. 100 ft. Lehigh / Yale, Crescent Blvd and the south-east plan left out.
